tagline.text: A clear mountain-stream waterfall and wide pool above Laurel, on the way to Ambon-Ambon Falls

location.label: Location
location.text: Sitio Salipit, Barangay San Gabriel (on the boundary with Barangay Paliparan), Laurel, Batangas

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱500~1,300 (per person, including round-trip transport from Manila; guide and cottage split among the group)

children.text: Malagaslas Falls lies in a stream valley inside Sitio Salipit, Barangay San Gabriel, in Laurel, Batangas. It is a 10 to 30 minute walk from the end of the village road, and many visitors swim in the large pool and then continue to Ambon-Ambon Falls on a half-day outing.

Malagaslas Falls is in the town of Laurel, on the western shore of Taal Lake. The Laurel municipal tourism page places it between Barangay Paliparan and Barangay San Gabriel, while travel blogs describe starting from Sitio Salipit in San Gabriel. OpenStreetMap has a point named
Malagaslas Spring
at roughly 14.05° N, 120.90° E. It sits close to Ambon-Ambon Falls farther up the same valley, which fits the accounts that the two are linked by a single trail.

According to the Laurel tourism page, the name comes from the Tagalog word "lagaslas," which describes the sound and force of fast-flowing water striking rocks, and a 2017 travel blog likewise traces it to the sound of the water. In reality the falls are less a single giant plunge than a series of small drops that spill in several tiers, with a large sandbagged pool at the bottom where a group can soak together. Three smaller pools are described farther upstream. The Laurel page says the water is so clear that it is safe to drink, but for safety travelers should bring their own drinking water.

What makes this place easy is how close it is. The municipal page says it is about 1 km, or a 10-minute walk, from Laurel Municipal Hall, and blog reports say the first falls appear within about 10 minutes of walking from the end of the Salipit village road. The municipal page also says it takes about 30 minutes on foot from the Hacienda Cascada entrance, so the walking time depends on which way you enter. It is a distance you can cover as a day trip from Manila, and combined with Ambon-Ambon Falls farther up the valley it fills a half day well.

The atmosphere is that of a modest local stream rather than a resort. There are bamboo cottages and small food stalls by the water, which makes it good for picnics, but there is no toilet right beside the falls, and some reports say nearby residents let visitors use their bathrooms for a fee. It is quiet early on weekday mornings and busier with families around midday on weekends. Fees, guide arrangements and road conditions differ from report to report, so treat the amounts in this article as rough guides and check the latest announcements before you go. If it is your first time, here is the mindset I recommend. This is not a big waterfall that overwhelms you in a single photo; it is a place to rest slowly beside clear water. The walk from the entrance is short, so it fits easily into any schedule, and its biggest advantage is that if you still have energy after relaxing in the pool, you can walk up to Ambon-Ambon Falls above. On the other hand, facilities are minimal and the stream changes a lot with the weather, so bring your own water, snacks and a change of clothes, and allow extra time. Laurel is on the western shore of Taal Lake, so after the falls you can easily add a lake viewpoint or head up to Tagaytay. There are also things to check before visiting. The starting points described by the Laurel tourism page and by blog reports (the Hacienda Cascada entrance and the Salipit village road) are different, so which route is open and where fees are collected may vary by season. Asking the Laurel municipal hall or the San Gabriel barangay hall in advance, or asking at the shop at the entrance when you arrive, is the most reliable approach. Some reports mention villagers who help arrange guides.

Malagaslas is a waterfall made of small drops stacked layer upon layer. True to its name, you hear the refreshing sound of water striking rock, and many reports say the water is clear enough to see the stones on the bottom.

blocks.title: A large pool held by sandbags

children.text: Below the falls there is a wide pool ringed with sandbags, ideal for a leisurely soak. Three smaller pools lie farther up, so even a big group can spread out.
A 2016 report says the way from the entrance to the falls includes a steel hanging bridge and a few shallow stream crossings. The path is short and fairly flat, and many people walk it with children.
Bamboo cottages and tables by the water make it easy to spread out a packed lunch and rest. A 2019 report lists roughly ₱300 for a cottage and ₱100 for a table, so check the current prices on site.

Higher up the same valley is Ambon-Ambon, a two-tier waterfall reported to be about 60 m high. It is said to be roughly 15 minutes farther on from Malagaslas, so if you have the energy I recommend going there as well.
At about 1 km from the municipal hall, it is an easy day trip from Manila. It also pairs well with a Taal volcano and lake viewing itinerary.
"Lagaslas" refers to the sound and force of water rushing over rocks. Part of the pleasure of coming here is that even with your eyes closed, the sound alone tells you what the name means.

items.title: Day trip from Manila
items.subtitle: Half-day trek to the Laurel falls

children.text: Take a bus toward Tanauan or Lipa from a Manila bus terminal such as Buendia. The closer to the first trip, the easier it is to avoid the midday heat.
Get off in central Tanauan, take a tricycle to the jeepney terminal, and transfer to a jeepney to Laurel. Reports say the ride to Laurel takes about
1 hour to 1 hour 30 minutes

From Laurel public market, take a tricycle to the entrance of Salipit village. Tell the driver you are going to the Malagaslas or Ambon-Ambon Falls entrance and he will understand. The road is reported to be bumpy and muddy when it rains.
Pay the entrance and registration fee at the small shop at the entrance and hire a local guide if you need one. Walk to the falls across the hanging bridge and streams.
Soak in the pool at Malagaslas Falls and have lunch at a cottage. There is no toilet beside the falls, so go beforehand.
If you have the energy, go on to Ambon-Ambon Falls. On the way up you have to cross a stream once more, and it can be dangerous after rain.
Return to the entrance and head back into Laurel town. The last jeepney leaves early, so check the return schedule first.

A 2016 report says the last jeepney to Talisay left at 3 PM. Schedules can change, so be sure to ask locally. The Laurel tourism page says it is about a 30-minute walk from the Hacienda Cascada entrance, and about 45 minutes to Ambon-Ambon from the entrance. Walking time depends on the starting point, so ask for directions.

items.title: Taal volcano combination
items.subtitle: Enjoy the falls and the lake over two days and one night

children.text: Enjoy the Taal volcano and lake itinerary from Tagaytay or Talisay.
Move to central Laurel, find lodging, and buy snacks and water at the market.
Head to Salipit early and see Malagaslas and Ambon-Ambon during the quiet hours.
Have lunch in Laurel and head back toward Manila.

items.title: From Manila by bus and jeepney

children.text: Take a bus toward Tanauan, Lipa or Batangas City from the Buendia or Pasay terminal in Manila. A 2016 report puts the Buendia to Tanauan fare at ₱95, with a ride of under 2 hours.
In Tanauan, take a tricycle (₱40 at the time) to the jeepney terminal and board a jeepney to Laurel (₱45 at the time).
From Laurel public market, take a tricycle to the Salipit village entrance. Reports say the one-way fare is at least ₱60~65.
Fares come from 2016 to 2017 reports and may be different now. Confirm with the driver before boarding.
From Manila, take SLEX and the STAR Tollway, exit at Tanauan, and head toward Laurel. Reports say you can park near the entrance.
The Salipit village road is bumpy and muddy after rain, so low cars should take care.
It is about 1 km from Laurel Municipal Hall, so people usually go by tricycle or motorcycle taxi.
The Laurel tourism page says that starting from the Hacienda Cascada entrance takes about 30 minutes on foot.
The dry season, January to May, is best. The water is clear, the stream crossings are easy, and it is safer to get in the pool.
In the rainy season the swollen streams and muddy road make access difficult, and sudden rises in water are dangerous. Postpone your trip if heavy rain is forecast.

Beware of swollen streams and muddy trails; avoid after heavy rain

There is hardly any lodging near the falls, so most people stay in central Laurel or in nearby Tagaytay or Talisay. There are also almost no restaurants right beside the falls, so buy snacks and water beforehand.
You can have a simple meal at local eateries around Laurel public market, such as lomi. One report lists a bowl of lomi at about ₱40.

On a day trip, it is best to plan your lunch and rest times around the schedule of your ride back to Manila. If you want to stay overnight, look first at lodging in central Laurel or on the Tagaytay side, and check room rates and availability yourself.
Bring swimwear, water shoes, a change of clothes and a towel. The rocks are slippery.
There is no toilet beside the falls, so go before you set out.
Bring cash in small change (₱5, ₱10, ₱20). The entrance and registration fee is collected at a small shop.
A guide is not required, but it is reassuring if it is your first time. Some reports mention dogs and snakes.
Weekday early mornings are the quietest.
Carry out all your trash.
Check the last jeepney time in advance.
Ask Laurel Municipal Hall for the latest entry arrangements and trail conditions. The municipal tourism page recommends hiring a guide because the trail winds.
If you plan to go on to Ambon-Ambon, water shoes and a waterproof bag help, and leave plenty of time for the return.
The stream can rise in an instant after rain, so do not go in if heavy rain is forecast or dark clouds hang over the upper valley.
Rocks and moss are slippery, so wear water shoes and walk slowly.
The pool is not uniformly deep, so adults should stay next to children.
The access road is bumpy and muddy when it rains.
Toilets and shops are scarce, so bring water and snacks.
Do not leave valuables unattended in the cottage.
A two-tier waterfall about 60 m high farther up the same valley, roughly
15 minutes
on foot from Malagaslas.
Laurel sits on the lakeshore, so you can enjoy views of the lake as well.
Famous for its volcano views and cafe strip, and easy to add to an itinerary by car from Laurel.
